title: The Lost Wallet
text:
On Tuesday I found a brown [[wallet]] on the sidewalk outside the bank. It was [[quite]] heavy. Inside there was money, some cards, and a photo of an old woman holding a baby.

I stood there for a moment, not [[sure]] what to do. Nobody was watching. My friend Ben said, "Just keep it. Nobody will ever know."

But something felt [[wrong]]. I could not [[really]] explain it. I [[always]] think about how I would feel if I lost something [[important]] like that.

So we walked into the bank [[together]] and gave it to the clerk at the counter. She looked [[surprised]] and asked for my name and phone number. I [[almost]] said no, but Ben told her anyway.

Three days later my mother called me to the phone. An old man was on the line. His [[voice]] was quiet and a little shaky. He said the wallet was his, and that the photo inside was of his wife and their first son. The money did not matter to him, but that photo could [[never]] be replaced.

He asked if he could thank me in person. On Saturday he came to our door with a box of moon cakes. He walked slowly with a stick, but his eyes were [[bright]].

"You did the [[correct]] thing," he said. "Not everybody would."

I [[still]] think about that afternoon [[sometimes]]. The moon cakes are long gone. What I remember is how [[glad]] I felt walking home.

title: My First Job
text:
Last summer I worked at a small [[bakery]] near the station. It was my first [[real]] job. I had to get up at five, which was [[terrible]] at first.

The owner, Mrs. Lin, was [[serious]] but [[helpful]]. On my first morning she showed me how to carry the trays without dropping them. "Do it slowly," she said. "[[Never]] run with hot bread."

The work was [[hard]]. My shoulders hurt for the first week. I [[often]] wanted to quit. But the smell of fresh bread at six in the morning was [[wonderful]], and the customers were [[usually]] kind.

An old woman came in at seven every single day and bought the same two rolls. After a week she started calling me by my name. Small things like that made the early mornings easier.

One morning I made a [[dangerous]] mistake. I left the oven door open and burned a whole tray. I thought Mrs. Lin would shout at me. She looked at the black bread, [[then]] at my face, and said, "Everybody does that [[once]]. Clean it up and start [[again]]."

By August I could do everything [[quite]] fast. I knew every kind of bread by name. [[Finally]], on my last day, Mrs. Lin gave me an [[envelope]] with my pay and a note inside. It said: "You were [[ready]] to learn. That is the most [[useful]] thing a person can be."

I keep that note in my drawer to this day.

title: The Night Market
text:
My cousin came from abroad last month, and I took her to the night [[market]] on Friday evening. She had [[never]] been to one before.

The street was [[so]] crowded that we had to walk one behind the other. The air was warm and full of noise. On both sides there were lights, [[loud]] music, and the smell of fried food.

We started at the entrance and worked our way down. Every few steps someone was calling out prices, and the steam from the food stalls rose into the lights above our heads. My cousin kept stopping to take photos of things I had walked past a hundred times without looking.

The first thing she wanted to try was stinky tofu. I told her the smell was [[strange]] but the taste was [[excellent]]. She was not [[sure]], but she tried a small piece. Her face turned red. "It is [[really]] good," she said, [[quite]] surprised.

We [[also]] ate oyster omelets, pineapple cake, and a bowl of shaved [[ice]] together. Everything was [[fresh]] and cheap. I spent [[almost]] all my money in one hour.

At a game stall I threw rings at bottles [[twice]] and won nothing. My cousin threw [[just]] one time and won a large toy bear. That was [[lucky]], and a little unfair.

By ten o'clock we were [[tired]] and our bags were heavy. Walking home, my cousin said the night market was the most [[interesting]] place she had seen in Taiwan.

"Do you come here [[often]]?" she asked.

"[[Seldom]]," I said. "But [[maybe]] I should."
